_about: Student-facing content for each quarter. One source: screens read only from here. Wording follows section 1A of the design (plain, conversational). {placeholders} are filled from the team's results.

briefing.headline: Your first quarter: find out what actually makes money
paragraphs: The old presidents' settings are still running. Fourteen drilling rigs are working in Texas, Baton Rouge is running at 96%, and Rotterdam is running at 82% after losing money in three of the last four quarters.
Marcus Delacroix thinks Rotterdam should be sold. Ingrid Vestergaard thinks Texas could drill more. Neither of them has shown you numbers that compare one part of Halden with another.
Oil prices slipped over the holidays. Grant Whitaker wants to know by Thursday whether you'll change anything this quarter, and why.
briefing.question: Which parts of Halden really make money, and how many rigs should drill in Texas?

1.rule: A rig costs $40 million a quarter. Each extra rig drills poorer ground than the one before, so it adds less oil. New wells take about three months to start pumping. In Norway, the government takes 78% of the profit on every barrel, and it also absorbs 78% of any loss. A refinery has costs that come with each barrel it runs and costs it pays whether it runs or not.
1.new_pages_note: This quarter you can change the oil fields and the refineries. Gas station prices open next quarter.

exhibits.title: The asset register: every oil field, refinery and gas station business, with its costs
Python notebook with the same data (optional)

1.marchetti: Oil dropped from $73 to $71 a barrel over the winter. Refining margins on the Gulf Coast held up, around $22 a barrel. Europe is weak: refiners near Rotterdam are making about $4 a barrel. I wouldn't plan on prices bouncing back quickly, but I wouldn't plan on a collapse either.

bands.title: Fewer rigs, more cash
paragraphs: You cut Texas to {rigs} rigs. Drilling spending fell, and free cash flow came in at {fcf}. Ingrid asked Grant why Texas was drilling less while oil was still above $70.
Texas output was {permian_prod} barrels a day this quarter. Fewer rigs means less new oil from next quarter on, so watch how fast that number slides.

bands.title: Steady as she goes
paragraphs: You kept Texas at about the old presidents' level, {rigs} rigs. Nothing surprised anyone, including Grant.
Texas output was {permian_prod} barrels a day. Whether each of those rigs earns back its $40 million is still an open question.

bands.title: Texas drilled hard
paragraphs: You pushed Texas to {rigs} rigs. Ingrid was delighted. Grant noticed that drilling spending jumped, and free cash flow came in at {fcf}.
The new wells start pumping next quarter. Each extra rig drilled poorer ground than the last one, so the question is whether they pay for themselves.

story.closing: Halden earned {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation this quarter. Next quarter, you'll also set prices at the gas stations.

news.title: Oil drifts lower
news.body: Crude slipped to about $71 a barrel. Most producers in your class kept drilling at last year's pace.

news.title: Rotterdam's neighbours struggle
news.body: European refiners are making about $4 a barrel. Two plants near Rotterdam cut their runs over the winter.

marcus.why: You went to Baton Rouge first.

ingrid.why: You met her first and listened.
You met Ingrid before him. He noticed.

briefing.headline: Danielle wants to cut prices. Elena wants to see the numbers first.
paragraphs: A rival chain has been running ads about cheaper gas across Louisiana. Danielle Roy says Cordell is losing drivers and wants to cut what Cordell charges its station owners everywhere.

Elena Marchetti says a few cents means very different things in a city with a station on every corner and in a small town with one station for miles. She's pulled four years of prices and sales by type of market.
Most Cordell stations are owned by dealers. You set what Cordell charges them. They decide what drivers pay.
briefing.question: What should Cordell charge its station owners in each kind of market, and what should Halden charge drivers in Europe?

2.rule: When you change what Cordell charges a dealer, the dealer passes part of it on to drivers. City dealers pass on about 82 cents of every dollar; small-town dealers about 42 cents. City drivers switch stations over a few cents; small-town drivers barely notice. If you keep a price rise in place, more drivers drift away each quarter. If you cut prices, rivals start matching you, so the extra drivers fade. In Europe, Halden owns its stations and sets the pump price directly.
2.new_pages_note: New this quarter: gas station prices.

exhibits.title: Four years of prices and sales, by type of market
Python notebook with the same data (optional)

2.marchetti: Oil is flat at about $70.50. What matters this quarter is how drivers react to price. In cities they react a lot. In small towns and on highways, hardly at all. One national price would be wrong almost everywhere.

bands.title: Cheaper gas, busier stations
paragraphs: You cut prices on average. Stations got busier in the cities, and Danielle sent the whole sales team a note of congratulations.
Fuel profit at Cordell came in at {cordell_fuel}. Rival chains noticed the cuts. Expect some of them to match you next quarter.

bands.title: Prices held
paragraphs: You left prices about where they were. Danielle thinks you missed a chance. Elena thinks you didn't have to change anything to find out what drivers would do.
Fuel profit at Cordell came in at {cordell_fuel}.

bands.title: Higher prices, fewer drivers where it counts
paragraphs: You raised prices on average. Fuel profit at Cordell came in at {cordell_fuel}. In the cities, a few drivers went elsewhere. In the small towns, almost nobody noticed.
Price rises that last tend to cost more drivers over time. Keep an eye on traffic.

story.closing: Halden earned {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation this quarter. Next quarter, Rotterdam's future is on the table.

news.title: Price war talk in Louisiana
news.body: Two chains cut street prices by a few cents in Baton Rouge and New Orleans. Small-town prices barely moved.

news.title: European margins tick up
news.body: Refiners around Rotterdam made a little over $5 a barrel this quarter, the best in a year.

down.why: You took her advice on prices.

flat.why: She asked for price cuts and didn't get them.

up.why: You raised prices while she was asking for cuts.

briefing.headline: Rotterdam asks to know its future
paragraphs: The works council in Rotterdam has written to Sandvik. They want to know whether the refinery has a future before they agree to the winter maintenance plan.

Bjørn Aasen says Rotterdam covers its running costs and should keep going. Marcus says it loses money every year and should be closed or sold. Straits Pacific, meanwhile, wants to know how hard you'd like Singapore to run this quarter.
You now have more choices for Rotterdam: keep running, pause it, or close it for good.
briefing.question: Should Rotterdam keep running, slow down, pause, or close?

3.rule: Rotterdam earns the European refining margin plus $1.50 a barrel, and spends $4.10 a barrel on costs that come with each barrel it runs. It also pays $2.30 a barrel of fixed costs (staff, upkeep) on its full size whether it runs or not. Pausing stops the per-barrel costs but not the fixed ones, plus $5 million a quarter of care costs. Restarting after a pause costs $85 million. Closing costs $150 million once and is permanent. Singapore is a request: Straits Pacific owns 60% and decides.
3.new_pages_note: New this quarter: pause or close Rotterdam, and what you ask Singapore for.

exhibits.title: What each refinery spends, per barrel and fixed
What it would take to restart Rotterdam
Refining margins month by month, three regions
Who decides what at the Singapore joint venture
Worked example: a refinery deciding whether to run

3.marchetti: Oil is up a little, to about $72.60. Europe's refining margin is near $4.90 a barrel, better than last winter but still thin. If you're deciding about Rotterdam, the number to compare it with isn't whether it makes a profit. It's whether it covers the costs that stop when it stops.

bands.title: Rotterdam is closing
paragraphs: You closed Rotterdam. The one-time cost hit this quarter, and the works council has asked for a meeting with Sandvik.
Halden no longer carries Rotterdam's losses. It also no longer earns anything from Europe's refining margin, whatever happens to it from here.

bands.title: Rotterdam goes quiet
paragraphs: You paused Rotterdam. The plant stopped buying crude, but the staff, the upkeep and the care costs are still on the books: Rotterdam cost {rotterdam} this quarter.
Restarting will cost $85 million. Bjørn has asked how long you expect the pause to last.

bands.title: Rotterdam runs on
paragraphs: You kept Rotterdam running hard. It still lost money after its fixed costs ({rotterdam} this quarter), but less than it would have running slowly.
The works council has agreed to the maintenance plan. Marcus says you're throwing good money after bad. Bjørn says you're the first person in years to understand the plant.

bands.title: Rotterdam, slowed down
paragraphs: You kept Rotterdam running, but slowly. It lost {rotterdam} this quarter after its fixed costs.
Bjørn warns that equipment run slowly for a long time starts to act up. The works council is still waiting for an answer.

story.closing: Straits Pacific ran Singapore at {sg_accepted}%. Halden earned {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation this quarter. Next quarter, Geneva's results raise a question about how Halden charges itself for crude.

news.title: European refiners pick different paths
news.body: Some companies in your class slowed or paused their European refineries this quarter. Others kept running. Traders are watching what that does to Europe's refining margin.

news.title: Singapore partners stay cautious
news.body: Asian refining margins were steady at a little over $12 a barrel.

closed.why: You closed a plant he spent 20 years running.
He's wanted Rotterdam gone for years.

idle.why: He doesn't trust a pause to stay a pause.

running_hard.why: You kept the plant he wants to sell.

running_slow.why: He thinks running slowly is the worst of both.

briefing.headline: Geneva just had its best quarter in four years
paragraphs: Lorenz Kuhn's trading desk in Geneva just had its best quarter in four years. Marcus Delacroix noticed first. About half of Geneva's profit came from one trick: buying Texas crude cheaply on the open market while Baton Rouge kept paying Halden's own, higher price for it.

Marcus wants the price Baton Rouge pays to be what the crude actually costs to pump and ship. The oil fields team wants it to stay at the market price. Kuhn says he's fine either way, and that's exactly what worries Grant Whitaker, the CFO.
briefing.question: How much should Baton Rouge pay Halden's own oil fields for Texas crude?

4.rule: When Halden's own crude price is different from the outside market price, Geneva can trade on the gap. It keeps 35 cents of every dollar of difference, on up to 40,000 barrels a day, and that shows up as Geneva's profit. Here's the key point: the price doesn't change what Halden earns in total. It only changes which part of Halden gets the credit.
4.new_pages_note: New this quarter: what Baton Rouge pays for Texas crude, on your Trading & finance page. It stays there for the rest of the course.

4.marchetti: Oil is at $74 a barrel, and traders expect it to stay about there. What I keep looking at is Europe: refineries there are making only $4.60 on each barrel, and the ones around Rotterdam are slowing down. Honestly, I don't have a call on next quarter's oil price that I'd bet a refinery on.

bands.title: Baton Rouge's best quarter since the merger
paragraphs: Baton Rouge had its best quarter since the merger. Marcus sent the plant a thank-you note and made sure you were copied. Meanwhile, the oil fields' profit dropped to almost nothing on paper, and Ingrid asked Grant why.
Geneva stopped making money on the gap in Halden's own crude prices. Kuhn didn't mention it.

bands.title: Nothing changed, and everyone noticed
paragraphs: You kept the market price the old presidents used. The oil fields had a strong quarter on paper. Baton Rouge's numbers stayed thin, and Marcus sent you an email complaining about it, with the CEO copied.
Geneva had a quiet quarter. Kuhn didn't complain.

bands.title: Geneva had another great quarter
paragraphs: You moved the price, but only partway. The oil fields and Baton Rouge both posted so-so numbers, and neither side was happy.
Geneva made {geneva} on the gap between your price and the outside market. Kuhn sent Grant a short note about it. Grant forwarded it to you without a word.

story.closing: Here's the thing: Halden as a whole made {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation, exactly what it would have made at any price. The money just moved from one column to another. Next on Grant's mind: currencies, before the Norwegian krone moves again.

news.title: Lenders are asking about internal prices
news.body: Several companies in your class changed what their refineries pay for their own crude this quarter. Banks have started asking about it when they review loans.

news.title: European refineries slowed down again
news.body: Several refineries around Rotterdam ran below 80% for another quarter. Traders say Europe can make more diesel than it can sell.

cost.why: You set Baton Rouge's crude price at cost. His refinery just had its best quarter since the merger.
The oil fields' profit collapsed on paper, and nobody asked her first.
Geneva can't make money on the price gap anymore.

market.why: You kept the old price after he'd asked you to change it.

between.why: Geneva made money on the gap you left.
He's asked twice why Geneva's profit keeps going up.

briefing.headline: The euro fell 6% over the holidays, and the krone fell with it
paragraphs: The dollar jumped while everyone was away. The euro dropped from $1.085 to $1.015, and the Norwegian krone weakened from 10.20 to 11.05 per dollar. Danielle says the European stations will look worse in dollars. Bjørn points out that Norway pays its people and suppliers in kroner. Ana says the board expects Halden to do something about it.

Grant Whitaker has agreed, for the first time, to let you hedge. You can sell part of next quarter's oil at today's price, and buy or sell euros and kroner for next quarter at today's rates. He wants to know which of Halden's currency risks are real before you use any of it.
One more thing on the prices page: European refining margins have moved a lot since last summer, after refiners around Rotterdam changed how hard they ran.
briefing.question: Which of Halden's currency risks are real, and how much, if any, should you hedge?

5.rule: A weaker krone makes Norway's costs cheaper in dollars, because those costs are paid in kroner. A weaker euro shrinks what the European stations earn once it's turned into dollars. Rotterdam earns and spends in euros, so the two mostly cancel out. Any hedge you set this quarter settles next quarter: oil at this quarter's price, euros and kroner at today's rates. If prices then move in your favour, the hedge costs you; if they move against you, it pays. Grant lets you hedge up to half of next quarter's oil and up to $600 million of each currency.
5.new_pages_note: New this quarter: three hedges on your Trading & finance page. Grant has to agree to them, so each one has a limit.

exhibits.title: Where Halden's money is earned and spent, by currency
Python notebook with the same data (optional)

5.marchetti: The euro is at $1.015 and the krone at 11.05 per dollar. Forward markets think the euro could be back near $1.03 within a year, but I wouldn't bet the company on that. Oil is about $72. The question isn't which way currencies go next. It's which parts of Halden actually feel it.

bands.title: You let the currencies ride
paragraphs: You didn't hedge anything this quarter. The currency moves changed Halden's earnings by {fx_effect} on their own: Norway's costs got cheaper in dollars, the European stations earned less, and Rotterdam mostly cancelled itself out.
The euro hedge the old team set up last year paid {hedges}. Grant noticed you didn't use the hedging he'd agreed to.

bands.title: A measured first hedge
paragraphs: The currency moves changed Halden's earnings by {fx_effect} this quarter, before any hedging. Norway's costs got cheaper in dollars, the European stations earned less, and Rotterdam mostly cancelled itself out.
You hedged part of next quarter. Those hedges settle next quarter, at whatever oil and currencies do by then. The euro hedge the old team set up last year paid {hedges}.

bands.title: You used most of Grant's hedging limits
paragraphs: The currency moves changed Halden's earnings by {fx_effect} this quarter, before any hedging. Norway's costs got cheaper in dollars, the European stations earned less, and Rotterdam mostly cancelled itself out.
You used most of the limits Grant set. If oil or the euro moves your way next quarter, those hedges will cost real money. The euro hedge the old team set up last year paid {hedges}.

story.closing: Halden made {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation. Next on Ingrid's desk: three big projects, and not enough money for all of them.

news.title: The dollar is at a five-year high
news.body: The euro fell about 6% and the krone nearly 8% against the dollar. Companies that earn in dollars and spend in kroner are quietly better off.

news.title: European refining margins moved sharply
news.body: How hard refiners around Rotterdam ran last summer, including the companies in your class, is now showing up in what they earn on each barrel. Check this quarter's European margin on the prices page.

none.why: He agreed to let you hedge, and you didn't use it or explain why.

measured.why: You hedged carefully, well inside his limits.

heavy.why: You used nearly all of his hedging limits the first time you had them.

briefing.headline: Three projects, one budget
paragraphs: Ingrid has three projects ready for the board: an upgrade at Baton Rouge, an upgrade at Rotterdam, and Helix, a new business built around a West Texas supply contract with a customer in Rotterdam. Marcus wants Baton Rouge. Bjørn wants Rotterdam. Margrethe wants Helix.

There isn't money for all three. How much the board lets Ingrid spend, and what Halden's money costs this quarter, depend on how lenders now read the industry, including how companies like Halden priced their own crude last autumn.
briefing.question: Which of the three projects should Halden go ahead with, given what money costs this quarter?

6.rule: Each project costs its full price now and pays back over about ten years. Once you go ahead with one, there's no turning back. The board caps what Ingrid can spend this quarter, and Halden's cost of capital sets what money in later years is worth today. Forecasts run optimistic: refining upgrades have delivered about 88% of what was promised, new businesses about 61%. A project's price adds to Halden's debt, but your free cash flow score is measured before new projects, so a good project isn't punished in the quarter you pay for it.
6.new_pages_note: New this quarter: Big projects, a page for the EVP.

Lenders are pricing companies' money off how disciplined they've been with their own numbers, and that changes which project looks best. Work out what each one is worth at this quarter's cost of capital before you rank them.

bands.title: You kept the money in the bank
paragraphs: You didn't go ahead with any of the three projects. Ingrid told the board Halden would wait. Marcus, Bjørn and Margrethe each asked you why, separately.
The hedges you set last quarter settled at {hedges}.

bands.title: The refineries get the money
paragraphs: You committed {project_outlay} to refining upgrades. They start paying next quarter, at whatever they really deliver. Margrethe asked whether Halden had just decided what it wants to be.
The hedges you set last quarter settled at {hedges}.

bands.title: You bet on Helix
paragraphs: You committed {project_outlay}, with Helix at its centre. It's slow to start, and most of its money comes in later years. Marcus called it a science project. Margrethe called you to say well done.
The hedges you set last quarter settled at {hedges}.

story.closing: Halden made {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation. Next quarter, a rival chain makes a move on prices, and you'll see how every measure compares with the rest of the class.

news.title: Lenders are rewarding discipline
news.body: Banks have started setting what they charge oil companies by how carefully those companies price their own internal deals. Last autumn's choices across your class are now in this quarter's cost of capital.

news.title: The euro steadied
news.body: The euro recovered to about $1.031. Companies that sold euros forward at the bottom gave some of it back.

none.why: She prepared three projects and you sent her back to the board with none.

refining.why: She wanted to see Halden try something new.

helix.why: You backed the new business she's been pushing for.
He thinks Helix took Baton Rouge's money.

briefing.headline: Pelican cuts prices and announces a refinery
paragraphs: Pelican Energy, the Gulf Coast refiner with its own chain of stations, cut what drivers pay by six cents a gallon on Friday, in every kind of market where Cordell has stations. Marcus had the city dealers on the phone by Saturday. They want Cordell to match.

On Monday Pelican announced a new refining unit on the Gulf Coast. Ana's team thinks it's a real plan. Bjørn thinks it's a bluff meant to make Halden think twice about its own Baton Rouge upgrade. Grant wants to know what it costs to be wrong either way.
It's also the midterm. When this quarter's results come in, you'll see how every one of your seven measures compares with the other teams in your class.
briefing.question: Where, if anywhere, should Cordell match Pelican's price cut, and should Halden answer Pelican's refinery with one of its own?

7.rule: Pelican has cut what drivers pay by six cents a gallon near Cordell stations in all four kinds of market. In any market where you hold your price, some drivers switch to Pelican: the more stations nearby, the more switch. Where you match, Cordell gives up six cents on every gallon it sells there and keeps its drivers. Pelican has also announced a new refining unit on the Gulf Coast. If Pelican builds and you don't, Baton Rouge loses some margin. If you both build, you both lose more. If you build and Pelican backs off, you gain. You'll find out next quarter what Pelican really does, and whatever you decide about building is for good.
7.new_pages_note: New this quarter: how to answer Pelican's cut, market by market, on the Gas stations page, and whether to answer its refinery on the Big projects page.

7.marchetti: Oil is at $75, and the Gulf Coast refining margin has slipped to $21.40 a barrel. A price cut and a capacity announcement in the same week aren't a coincidence: Pelican wants Halden looking at two things at once. Work out what each one costs you if you do nothing, before you decide what to do.

bands.title: You held your prices
paragraphs: Pelican cut six cents a gallon across Cordell's markets and you held every price. Some drivers drifted. It cost about {ignore_cost} of fuel and shop profit this quarter, less than most people in Houston expected. Marcus's city dealers called him all month anyway.
{capacity_answer}

bands.title: You matched in some markets and held in others
paragraphs: Where you matched Pelican, Cordell gave up six cents on every gallon it sold: {match_cost} this quarter. Where you held, drivers drifting to Pelican cost about {ignore_cost}. Marcus says you picked the right markets. Danielle says you picked the wrong ones.
{capacity_answer}

bands.title: You went to war
paragraphs: You matched Pelican's cut in most or all of Cordell's markets. That kept the drivers and gave up {match_cost} of fuel margin this quarter. Pelican noticed. So did every other chain on the Gulf Coast, and the shop counters went quiet: drivers who shop on price don't stop for coffee.
{capacity_answer}

story.closing: Halden made {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation. Your score page now shows where every measure sits against the rest of the class. Next quarter your team swaps seats, and OPEC+ meets in Vienna.

news.title: Price cuts spread along the Gulf Coast
news.body: Pelican's six-cent cut has some chains matching and others holding. Station owners say a price war empties the coffee counter: the drivers it wins are the ones who don't buy anything else. What the chains in your class did this quarter will show up in shop margins over the winter.

news.title: Refiners announce, analysts doubt
news.body: Pelican's Gulf Coast unit is the third expansion announced on the coast this year. Analysts expect about two of every three such announcements to turn into steel. Each one that does trims the margin every Gulf Coast refinery earns.

held.why: His city dealers wanted a fight and you held the price.
You didn't give away margin to win a quarter.

mixed.why: You matched where his dealers were loudest and held elsewhere.

matched.why: You gave up six cents on nearly every gallon. He's asking what it bought.
His dealers got the fight they asked for.

{capacity_answer}.hold: On the refinery, you let Pelican's announcement stand and built nothing. You'll find out next quarter whether they meant it.
{capacity_answer}.match: On the refinery, you answered Pelican's announcement with a new unit of your own at Baton Rouge. You'll find out next quarter whether they meant it.

briefing.headline: OPEC+ meets in Vienna, and your team has new jobs
paragraphs: Two things happened over the summer. Your team swapped seats: everyone now looks after a part of Halden they haven't run before, and the EVP chair has a new occupant. And OPEC+ called a meeting in Vienna for the end of November to agree a production cut.

If the cut holds, crude goes up. Lorenz in Geneva wants to buy crude for Baton Rouge now, before the meeting, and bank the rise. Marcus wants nothing of the sort: dearer crude squeezes his refinery, and he doesn't trust OPEC+ to deliver. Kwame has the history of past cuts on his desk. Elena has the odds.
You'll decide how much crude Geneva buys ahead, and what else to set across the company, without knowing which way Vienna goes. The answer arrives with your results.
briefing.question: What should Halden plan for at the OPEC+ meeting, and how should each part of the company be set so the whole company comes out ahead whichever way it goes?

8.rule: Prices this quarter are shown before the meeting: oil at $74 and the Gulf Coast margin at $21.50. Three things can happen in Vienna. The cut holds in full and oil goes to about $88. It partly holds and oil goes to about $81. It falls apart and oil slips to about $70. For every dollar crude rises, the Gulf Coast refining margin falls about 35 cents in the short run, so what helps the oil fields hurts Baton Rouge. Drivers barely notice: about 60 cents of each dollar reaches the pump, and volume moves a fraction of a percent. Geneva can buy crude for Baton Rouge ahead of the meeting at today's price: 30 days' worth if you plan for the cut to hold, 15 if you plan for a partial cut, none if you plan for it to fail. Crude bought ahead gains if oil rises and loses if it falls, and the money tied up costs interest. Hedges you set this quarter settle next quarter, as always. Gulf Coast refiners that added capacity last spring, including companies in your class, are also now in the margin.
8.new_pages_note: New this quarter: what Geneva plans for, on the Trading & finance page. Grant and Lorenz have to agree to it. Your team's seats have changed; check Your team in the left column.
8.rotation_note: Your team swapped seats this quarter. Everyone now looks after a part of Halden they haven't run before. The pages you can edit haven't changed; who's expected to lead on each one has.

exhibits.title: The three OPEC+ outcomes, how a crude move reaches each part of Halden, and what past cuts delivered

8.marchetti: Oil is at $74 going into Vienna. Weighting the three outcomes by the odds the market is pricing gives an expected $80.70, but nobody gets the expected price; you get one of the three. Work out what each outcome does to each part of Halden before you decide what to plan for, and look hardest at the one that hurts.

bands.title: The cut held
paragraphs: OPEC+ agreed the full cut in Vienna and, for once, delivered it. Oil jumped to {wti}. The oil fields had their best quarter since you took the job. Baton Rouge's margin fell to {gc} a barrel, and Marcus sent you a one-line note: told you so, about the margin, not the cut.
{opec_plan}

bands.title: The cut partly held
paragraphs: OPEC+ agreed its cut, and about half of it showed up in the market. Oil rose to {wti}. The oil fields earned more, Baton Rouge's margin eased to {gc} a barrel, and the stations barely noticed.
{opec_plan}

bands.title: The cut fell apart
paragraphs: OPEC+ announced a cut and then its members quietly pumped anyway. Oil slipped to {wti}. Baton Rouge's margin widened to {gc} a barrel, and Marcus was in a good mood for the first time since July. The oil fields were not.
{opec_plan}

story.closing: Halden made {ebitda} before interest, tax and depreciation. Next quarter, Danielle brings a proposal to put the Halden name on Cordell's stations, and the shop counters tell you what the price war did.

{opec_plan}.full: You planned for the cut to hold, so Geneva bought 30 days of Baton Rouge's crude ahead of the meeting. That came out at {bought_ahead}, after {inventory_carry} of interest on the money tied up.
{opec_plan}.partial: You planned for a partial cut, so Geneva bought 15 days of Baton Rouge's crude ahead of the meeting. That came out at {bought_ahead}, after {inventory_carry} of interest on the money tied up.
{opec_plan}.fails: You planned for the cut to fail, so Geneva bought nothing ahead. Lorenz says you left money on the table; Grant says you kept it in the bank. Both are describing the same quarter.

news.title: Vienna, and what it did to the Gulf Coast
news.body: Oil moved on the OPEC+ decision, and refining margins on the Gulf Coast moved the other way, as they usually do in the short run. On top of that, the refiners that added capacity last spring, including companies in your class, are now running those units, and every refinery on the coast is sharing the margin with them. Check the Gulf Coast margin on the Prices page.

news.title: Drivers shrug
news.body: Pump prices moved about 60 cents for every dollar on crude, and fuel sales hardly changed. Fuel is the last thing people stop buying. The shop counters are a different story, and they'll show next quarter.

full.why: Crude went up and Geneva had a good quarter.
His margin took the hit he warned about.

partial.why: A middling quarter for the desk.

fails.why: Cheap crude and a wide margin. He thinks you listened to him.
He wanted to buy ahead and the market went against him.
